981.title: Tsongkhapa
981.hook: the founder of the Gelug school: renunciation, bodhicitta, right view
981.howItsDone: Students in the Gelug school recite Tsongkhapa's Three Principal Aspects of the Path, hear it taught by their teachers, and study his Great Treatise on the Stages of the Path as a map of the whole way.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Longchenpa, and the mind's natural state, clear water when the stirring stops. When did you set your mind down like a glass? Day nine hundred eighty-one.

Here's a hard question for a slow evening. Out of everything you've ever been taught, if you could keep only three things, which would they be? Not three facts. Three things that hold the rest together. A Tibetan monk once answered that question for the whole Buddhist path. He wrote a long, careful book on the stages of the way to awakening. He also wrote a short poem that boils it down to three. Today, Tsongkhapa.
screen: `KEEP ONLY THREE THINGS.` → `A LONG BOOK ON THE PATH.` → `AND A SHORT POEM.`

segments.voice: First, the man. Tsongkhapa is remembered as the founder of the Gelug school. Tradition says he studied with teachers from several Tibetan lineages, prized monastic discipline and careful reasoning, and wrote the Great Treatise on the Stages of the Path. His short poem is called the Three Principal Aspects of the Path, and tradition says he wrote it as a letter to a student far away. Second, renunciation. Not throwing everything away, but a clear decision to be free: seeing that chasing one more comfort never ends the restlessness, and turning toward something steadier. Third, bodhicitta, the wish to awaken for the sake of all beings. The poem's logic is plain. Renunciation alone could become a private escape. Bodhicitta turns the journey outward, so the freedom sought is freedom for everyone, your neighbors included. Fourth, right view: understanding emptiness, that things arise in dependence on causes and do not stand on their own. Without it, the poem says, even renunciation and bodhicitta cannot cut the root of suffering. Put it in everyday terms. A traveler needs a reason to leave home, someone to make the trip for, and a true map. Leave out any one and the journey stalls. In the Gelug school, students learn this short text and come back to it, the long book folded into a pocket.
screen: `A LONG BOOK, AND A LETTER-POEM.` · `RENUNCIATION: DECIDING TO BE FREE.` · `BODHICITTA: FREEDOM FOR EVERYONE.` · `RIGHT VIEW: NOTHING STANDS ALONE.` · then, large: `A REASON, A PERSON, A MAP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name your three principal things. Settle, and give the breath a few slow rounds. Ask, quietly, what you want to be free of. Not a list, just one honest answer. Rest with it. Then ask who you'd want that freedom for, besides yourself. Let a face or two appear. Then ask what you'd need to see clearly for any of it to work. Let the answer be simple, even unfinished. Three questions, three short answers. You don't have to use Tsongkhapa's words. Notice what yours are. The bell holds the time.
Tsongkhapa. The founder of the Gelug school, who folded the whole path into three principal aspects: renunciation, bodhicitta and right view. Today's word.
Your line: three principal things. Today, before one real choice, run it past all three: what it frees you from, who else it serves, and whether you're seeing it clearly. Day nine hundred eighty-one.

pairs: a clear decision to be free
awakening for the sake of all beings
the long book on the stages of the path

options: nothing, that's enough
the wish to awaken for everyone, and right view

fork.reveal: in the poem, renunciation alone can become a private escape; bodhicitta and right view complete the path.

original.note: Sanskrit bodhicitta: the mind set on awakening for the sake of all beings, the second of the three.

trapdoor: what you thought: three good habits for a calmer life.
what it means: renunciation, bodhicitta and right view, the whole Buddhist path in three principal aspects.

982.title: The Karmapas
982.hook: the line of the Karmapas, heads of a Kagyu school, recognized life after life
982.howItsDone: In the Karma Kagyu school, the Karmapa is honored as the head of the lineage; practitioners recite lineage prayers naming past Karmapas, and recognized tulkus are trained from childhood by senior teachers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tsongkhapa, and your line: three principal things. Which choice did you run past all three? Day nine hundred eighty-two.

A sealed letter, kept safe by a teacher's closest students after his death. Inside, the stories say, are clues: the name of a valley, the shape of a house, the names of a child's parents. Search parties set out to follow them. Somewhere, a small boy is found, tested, and brought to a monastery, where he is honored as the same teacher, returned. In the Karma Kagyu school, the stories say, this has happened again and again. Today, the Karmapas.
screen: `A SEALED LETTER OF CLUES.` → `A SEARCH PARTY SETS OUT.` → `THE SAME TEACHER, RETURNED.`

segments.voice: First, the line. The Karmapas are the heads of the Karma Kagyu, one of the Kagyu schools that grew from the stream of Marpa, Milarepa and Gampopa. Each Karmapa is recognized as the rebirth of the one before, so the line runs life after life. Second, the word for such a teacher: tulku, a Tibetan word for an emanation body. Tibetan Buddhist teaching holds that an awakened teacher can choose to be reborn, out of compassion, to keep teaching. A tulku is not just a clever child. In the tradition's understanding, it is the same stream of mind taking up its work again. Third, how one is found. Tradition says Karmapas have often left letters describing where they would be reborn, and that senior teachers read the signs, search, and confirm. The child is then raised and trained, sometimes from a very young age, to become the teacher the school believes he already is. The Karmapa is also linked to a black crown, worn in a ceremony that devotees say brings blessing to all who see it. Fourth, honesty about a hard chapter. In recent times, different groups within the tradition have recognized different candidates for the same Karmapa, and that question has caused real pain among practitioners. This lesson takes no side. What stays the same in both cases is the idea at the center: a teaching held not only in books, but in a living line of people, passed from hand to hand.
screen: `HEADS OF THE KARMA KAGYU.` · `TULKU: AN EMANATION BODY.` · `LETTERS, SIGNS, A SEARCH.` · `A HARD CHAPTER, NO SIDE TAKEN.` · then, large: `A LIVING LINE OF PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn about one lineage. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one thing you know how to do: a recipe, a trade, a prayer, a way of fixing things. Ask who taught it to you. See that person. Then ask, if you know, who taught them. Go back as far as you can, one face at a time, even if the line soon disappears into people you never met. Notice that what you carry came through many hands. On the out-breath, let a little thanks run back along the line. The bell holds the time.
The Karmapas. The heads of the Karma Kagyu school, each recognized as the rebirth of the one before, a teacher returning life after life. Today's word.
Your line: life after life. Today, ask one person who taught them something they still do, and listen to the whole line. Day nine hundred eighty-two.

983.title: The wandering teacher
983.hook: Patrul Rinpoche, who wandered as a beggar and taught anyone
983.howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhist students, especially in the Nyingma school, read Patrul Rinpoche's Words of My Perfect Teacher as a guide to the preliminary practices, and stories of his humility are retold by teachers as examples.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Karmapas, a teacher found and recognized life after life, with a crown and a monastery waiting. Your line was life after life. Whose line of teachers did you hear about? Today, a teacher who wanted none of that. Day nine hundred eighty-three.

Tibetans tell a story about a traveling lama with a large party and a lot of baggage. On the road he meets a scruffy old man in a worn sheepskin coat and puts him to work: fetch the water, boil the tea, carry the bags. The old man does it all, cheerfully. Days later, at a great gathering, the lama walks in to hear the teacher everyone has come for, and the one on the high seat is the old man in the sheepskin coat. The lama, the story says, wanted the ground to swallow him. Today, the wandering teacher.
screen: `A LAMA WITH A LOT OF BAGGAGE.` → `AN OLD MAN BOILS THE TEA.` → `THE OLD MAN ON THE HIGH SEAT.`

segments.voice: First, who he was. The old man in those stories is Patrul Rinpoche, a Tibetan teacher remembered across the Nyingma school and beyond. He was recognized as a tulku, like yesterday's Karmapas, and could have lived surrounded by honor. Instead he spent much of his life wandering, often alone, dressed like a beggar, sleeping in caves and in the open. Second, what he taught, and to whom. He taught anyone who asked: monks, nomads, children. Tradition remembers him teaching Shantideva's Guide to the Bodhisattva's Way of Life over and over, so that ordinary people knew it well. And he wrote Words of My Perfect Teacher, a book on the foundations of practice, full of plain speech and sharp humor, which Tibetan students still read. Third, how he treated gifts. The stories say that when people offered him silver or fine things, he left them lying where they were, or gave them away, and moved on with almost nothing. The point is not that gifts are bad, or that the givers were wrong to give. The point is that he had nothing to guard, so nothing could hold him in one place. Fourth, why beggar teacher fits. For Patrul, humility wasn't a pose. It was a way of keeping the teaching free of the teacher. If nobody bows to the coat, then people have to listen to the words.
screen: `A TULKU WHO CHOSE THE ROAD.` · `HE TAUGHT ANYONE WHO ASKED.` · `GIFTS LEFT WHERE THEY LAY.` · `NOTHING BEING GUARDED.` · then, large: `THE BEGGAR TEACHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be humble today. Settle, and let the breath go soft. Bring to mind a moment when you wanted credit: a job done well, a kindness nobody noticed, an idea someone else got praised for. Notice how much you wanted to be seen, without judging it. Then, on the out-breath, set the credit down, the way Patrul left gifts where they lay. Now think of one helpful thing you could do today without anyone knowing it was you. Picture doing it, and walking away. The bell holds the time.
The wandering teacher. Patrul Rinpoche, a tulku who chose the road, dressed like a beggar, and taught anyone who asked. Today's word.
Your line: the beggar teacher. Today, do one good thing and let nobody find out it was you. Day nine hundred eighty-three.

984.title: Zhiyi
984.hook: the founder of Tiantai, who ordered all the sutras into one great system
984.howItsDone: In Tiantai (Tendai in Japan, Cheontae in Korea) communities, practitioners study the Lotus Sutra and Zhiyi's writings and practice calming and contemplation meditation as he described it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Patrul Rinpoche, the beggar teacher in the sheepskin coat. Did you manage one good thing nobody traced back to you? Today the story moves east, to China. Day nine hundred eighty-four.

A lot of kitchens have that one drawer. Batteries, twist ties, a key to nothing, a stack of takeout menus, a birthday candle. Everything in it is useful, and nothing can be found. Chinese Buddhists once had a drawer like that, only it was full of sutras. Teachings arrived from India and Central Asia over a long time, translated by different people, in no particular order. Some seemed simple, some soaring, and some seemed to say opposite things. Which one came first? Which one was the heart? A monk on a mountain set out to sort the whole drawer. Today, Zhiyi.
screen: `THAT ONE KITCHEN DRAWER.` → `A DRAWER FULL OF SUTRAS.` → `A MONK SETS OUT TO SORT IT.`

segments.voice: First, the man and the mountain. Zhiyi is honored as the founder of the Tiantai school, which takes its name from Mount Tiantai, where he lived and taught. Second, the sorting. Zhiyi's answer to the contradictions was not to throw any sutra out. Instead he arranged them as stages of the Buddha's teaching life, and as different kinds of teaching for different listeners. A doctor gives one patient a mild medicine and another a strong one, and both are right. In his scheme, the simpler sutras prepare the way, and the Lotus Sutra stands at the summit, where all the paths turn out to be one. Third, the practice behind the system. Zhiyi was not only a librarian of ideas. His lectures on meditation, written down by a student, are called Mohe Zhiguan, the great calming and contemplation. Calming settles the mind, like still water. Contemplation looks clearly at what's there. He taught them as two wings of one bird, and he wrote practical advice on posture, food, sleep and breath. Fourth, what a system is for. For Zhiyi, putting every teaching in its place was a kind of respect. Nothing was wasted, nothing was rejected, every sutra had a job. Other Chinese schools sorted the sutras differently, and Tiantai's order was not the only one. But his drawer, once sorted, could be opened by anyone.
screen: `A MONK ON MOUNT TIANTAI.` · `STAGES AND KINDS OF TEACHING.` · `CALMING AND CONTEMPLATION.` · `EVERY SUTRA HAS A JOB.` · then, large: `EVERYTHING IN ITS PLACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sort one messy thing, and today that thing is the mind. Settle, and let the breath calm down. That's the calming. Now, as each thought arrives, give it a quiet label and set it on a shelf. Planning. Remembering. Worrying. Hearing. Nothing gets thrown out. Each one just gets put where it belongs, and you come back to the breath. If the same thought keeps returning, label it again, gently. That's the contemplation: seeing clearly what's there. The bell holds the time.
Zhiyi. The founder of the Tiantai school, who ordered the sutras into one system with the Lotus Sutra at the summit, and taught calming and contemplation. Today's word.
Your line: everything in its place. Today, sort one messy drawer, shelf or inbox, and throw out less than you expected. Day nine hundred eighty-four.

985.title: The golden lion
985.hook: Fazang explains Huayan to the empress with a golden lion, and a room of mirrors
985.howItsDone: In Huayan and related traditions in China, Korea and Japan, students study the Flower Garland Sutra and Fazang's Essay on the Golden Lion, and teachers still use images like Indra's net and facing mirrors to explain how all things interpenetrate.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Zhiyi, who sorted the sutras and gave everything its place. What did you sort, and what did you decide to keep? Day nine hundred eighty-five.

A sutra so vast that an imperial court can't get hold of it. So the empress of China, who rules in her own name, asks a monk to explain it. Tradition says the monk doesn't open a book. He points across the palace hall to a statue standing there, a lion made of gold, and begins to talk about it. On another day, tradition says, he lines a room with mirrors, facing one another on every side, and sets a lamp and an image of the Buddha in the middle. Then he invites her in. Today, the golden lion.
screen: `AN EMPRESS ASKS A MONK.` → `A LION MADE OF GOLD.` → `A ROOM LINED WITH MIRRORS.`

segments.voice: First, the teacher. The monk is Fazang, a master of the Huayan school, named for the Flower Garland Sutra, and the empress is Wu Zetian. Second, the lion. Fazang asks her to look at it two ways. There is the gold, which has no shape of its own, and there is the lion, the shape the gold has taken. Without gold there's no lion. Without some shape, the gold isn't anything you can see. In his essay on the golden lion, the gold stands for the deep nature of things, and the lion stands for the world of particular things. They are not two. And more: every part of the lion is gold, so each single hair of the lion, the essay says, holds the whole lion. Third, the mirrors. Stand in that room and the lamp appears in every mirror, and in every mirror's reflection of every other mirror, without end. Huayan teaches that the world is like this: each thing reflects every other, and holds them all inside it. The Flower Garland Sutra is linked with an image of the same idea, a net hung with jewels, each jewel shining with the light of all the rest. Fourth, why it matters on an ordinary day. In Huayan's picture, if every thing contains every other thing, then no one is a side character. The neighbor, the stranger on the stairs, the person you argued with: in this teaching, each one holds a reflection of the whole, and so does the one listening.
screen: `FAZANG, THE EMPRESS, AND HUAYAN.` · `THE GOLD AND THE LION ARE NOT TWO.` · `A LAMP IN EVERY MIRROR.` · `NO ONE IS A SIDE CHARACTER.` · then, large: `MIRRORS IN MIRRORS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at a reflection in a reflection. If there's a window, a phone screen or a glass near you, look at how it holds the room, and how something in the room might hold it back. If not, close your eyes. Bring one person to mind, and then notice who is reflected in them: who raised them, who taught them, who fed them. Then notice yourself reflected there too. Let the reflections run on as far as they go, then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
The golden lion. Fazang's picture for the Huayan teaching: the gold and the shape are not two, and every part holds the whole, like mirrors in mirrors. Today's word.

Your line: mirrors in mirrors. Today, with one person you'd usually pass without a thought, remember Fazang's mirrors: in his picture, that person holds the whole room too. Day nine hundred eighty-five.

986.title: Mind is Buddha
986.hook: Mazu: this very mind is Buddha; later, no mind, no Buddha
986.howItsDone: In Chan and Zen communities, students meet Mazu's sayings and the Damei story as koans in collections such as the Gateless Gate, working with them in meditation and in private meetings with a teacher.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the golden lion, and Fazang's room of mirrors in mirrors. Whose reflection did you catch in a stranger? Today, a Chan teacher who points at something even closer. Day nine hundred eighty-six.

A monk comes to a Chan master with one question. What is Buddha? He might expect a lecture, a list, a sutra. Instead the teacher, Mazu, gives him a plain answer: this very mind is Buddha. The monk, the story says, woke up on the spot. He went off to live alone on a mountain called Damei, Great Plum, and the mountain's name became his. Years go by. Then a messenger arrives on the mountain with news. Mazu is teaching something different now. Today, mind is Buddha.
screen: `WHAT IS BUDDHA?` → `THIS VERY MIND IS BUDDHA.` → `NEWS REACHES THE PLUM MOUNTAIN.`

segments.voice: First, the teaching. Mazu was a Chan teacher in China, and a line tied to his name is this very mind is Buddha. Not a Buddha somewhere else, in another life, or in a statue. This mind, the one hearing these words, wondering about lunch. Second, the turn. Later, Mazu's students heard him say the opposite: no mind, no Buddha. Which is it? Chan records give his own explanation. Asked why he taught mind is Buddha, Mazu is said to have answered: to stop a child from crying. And when the crying stops? No mind, no Buddha. A teaching is a tool for a moment, not a slogan to cling to. Third, the plum. The messenger reaches Damei and tells him Mazu now teaches no mind, no Buddha. Damei answers, more or less, that the old man can keep confusing people as long as he likes. As for Damei, it's this very mind is Buddha. When Mazu heard this, the story says, he told his monks: the plum is ripe. Damei hadn't been holding a slogan. He'd seen for himself, so the new words couldn't shake him. Fourth, what it asks of anyone. Chan teachers in Mazu's line pointed to ordinary life, walking, eating, answering when your name is called, as the place to look. Nothing has to be added first. That can sound easy. In the stories, it rarely is.
screen: `THIS VERY MIND IS BUDDHA.` · `THEN: NO MIND, NO BUDDHA.` · `TO STOP A CHILD FROM CRYING.` · `THE PLUM IS RIPE.` · then, large: `THIS VERY MIND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice this mind, just as it is. Sit, and breathe normally. Ask the monk's question quietly, once: what is Buddha? Then drop the question, the way Mazu dropped his own words. See what the mind is doing right now. Busy, tired, waiting for the bell. When a thought comes, notice the plain fact that it is known. If an answer forms, a phrase or an idea, let it go too, like a toy handed to a crying child once the crying stops. Come back to this very mind, the one already here. The bell holds the time.
Mind is Buddha. Mazu's teaching that this very mind is Buddha, given to stop a child from crying, and later turned around: no mind, no Buddha. Today's word.
Your line: this very mind. Today, while you eat or walk, ask once: what is noticing this? Then finish the meal or the walk. Day nine hundred eighty-six.

987.title: Baizhang's rake
987.hook: old Baizhang keeps working; when his tools are hidden, he doesn't eat
987.howItsDone: In Zen and Chan monasteries, daily work called samu (in Japanese) is part of the schedule: residents and teachers share cleaning, cooking and garden work as practice, alongside sitting and chanting.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mazu, who said this very mind is Buddha, and later turned it upside down. Your line was this very mind. Where did you catch your own mind at work? Day nine hundred eighty-seven.

Morning in a Chinese mountain monastery, and the monks are heading out to the fields with hoes and rakes. Walking among them, slowly, is their teacher. He is old now, and the monks are worried about him. They have asked him to rest. He keeps coming anyway. So one night they do the only thing they can think of. They hide his tools. The next morning the teacher looks for them, finds nothing, and goes back to his room. At mealtime his bowl stays empty. He doesn't eat. Not that day, the story says, and not until the tools come back. His name was Baizhang, a student of Mazu, and today we follow him out to the field.
screen: `AN OLD TEACHER IN THE FIELDS.` → `THE MONKS HIDE HIS TOOLS.` → `THE BOWL STAYS EMPTY.`

segments.voice: First, what he said. When the monks asked why he wouldn't eat, the story has Baizhang answer with a short line, and it is the line he is remembered for: a day without work is a day without food. Your line comes from it. No work, no food. Second, what it is not. This isn't a boss counting hours, and it isn't a rule that people who can't work go hungry. Nobody was asking more of an old man. Baizhang asked it of himself. The work in the field was part of the practice, the same as the sitting and the chanting, and he would not be left out of it because of his age. Third, the community. Tradition credits Baizhang with shaping the rules for Chan monasteries, where everyone, teacher included, took a share of the daily labor: hauling water, cutting wood, working the fields. Later monastic codes carried his name. How much of the written code goes back to him is uncertain, so treat the details as tradition. The picture holds, though. In this kind of monastery, awakening was not only on the cushion. It was also at the end of a rake. Fourth, why the tools matter. The monks hid them out of love. Baizhang didn't scold anyone. He simply would not be excused from the practice. Sweeping, planting, washing the bowl: done fully, any of it can be the whole of the path for that hour.
screen: `A DAY WITHOUT WORK, A DAY WITHOUT FOOD.` · `ASKED OF HIMSELF, NOT OF OTHERS.` · `EVERYONE WORKS, TEACHER INCLUDED.` · `PRACTICE AT THE END OF A RAKE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one task, done fully. Settle and let the breath come and go. Pick a small piece of work from today, one you were going to rush. Washing a cup. Answering one email. Folding one shirt. Run it through slowly in your mind, from the first touch to the last. Notice the moment you usually start thinking about the next thing, and stay with this one instead. If you can, get up afterward and actually do it, start to finish, with nothing else in your hands. The bell holds the time.
Baizhang's rake. The old Chan teacher who kept working in the fields, and went without food when his tools were hidden. Today's word.
Your line: no work, no food. Today, before you eat one meal, do one piece of today's work fully, even if it's small, and notice how the food tastes after it. Day nine hundred eighty-seven.
